## Simple explanation

A cache stores copies of data that may be needed again, so later requests
can retrieve it faster or avoid repeating expensive work.

## Technical explanation

A cache is a storage layer between a data consumer and a slower or more
expensive source. It may keep database query results, computed values,
model outputs, or files. Cache design includes a key, an expiration or
invalidation policy, and a strategy for misses and concurrent updates.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

AI applications may cache embeddings, retrieval results, model responses,
or frequently used data to reduce latency and cost. Cached values can
become stale or expose data across users if keys and access boundaries are
not designed carefully.

## How it works

When a value is requested, the application checks the cache. A hit returns
the stored value; a miss fetches or computes the value from its source and
may store it for later. Expiration, invalidation, or eviction controls how
long entries remain available.

## Practical example

A service can cache a public configuration document after its first fetch.
Subsequent requests reuse the cached copy until it expires or the source
signals that it has changed.

## Common misconceptions

- A cache is not the authoritative source of data.
- Caching does not guarantee faster performance if the hit rate is low or
  cache access is costly.
- Cached AI responses must not be shared across users or contexts unless
  the cache key and privacy rules make that safe.
